doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Racial relations among bebop musicians and Gibbs' New York apartment parties
summary: Gibbs rejects the idea of racial motivation in bebop, says black and white musicians got along, and describes his large apartment where after-hours parties happened.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Okay. Before we move on from this part of your life, sometimes you read that one of the reasons that bebop became a new style of jazz is that black musicians were trying to weed out the white imitators and that there was a racial component to this music. And I wondered what your observation was back at that time?
I don’t believe that in the slightest bit because the feeling among the white and black musicians in the bebop era was the greatest feeling amongst human beings. We all got

along great. There was no problems at all. You know I used to have, I was very fortunate because visually, when you play vibes it’s like hearing and seeing a drummer. People don’t know if you’re good — when they see you do that — wonderful. You know? So I got puppy love, even though I made it pretty good, I got popular at an early age I think. Club owners made me a bandleader. First they would give me a band, then they let me have my own band. And I had a place on 57th Street and 10th Avenue in New York, it was like a big — like a football field room with a little bedroom and so you know everything used to close at 4:00 in the morning in New York, the clubs left at 4:00 in the morning. But I had this place and I used to go buy all these cheap bottles of liquor, bourbon was like 82 cents and I had bottles in my house. And after the job they’d say, “Hey let’s go to Gibbs’ house” and the place was packed at my house. I’d wake up in the morning and there were people sleeping there on the floor and I didn’t even know who they were, it was just whoever showed up it was party time. Because I was blessed. I was a band leader, I was making a decent salary, I had a good place, I was living in Manhattan, and so I was having a lot of fun. There was black and white musicians. Everybody was having a lot of fun.
